title: Private deployment network hardening: VPC patterns, firewall rules & mTLS
content:
Purpose:
This working doc captures recommended VPC layout patterns, firewall/security group rules, mTLS design guidance, and hardening checklists for Redwood Private deployments. It also outlines audit log schema considerations, SIEM export points, and evidence automation runbooks used for compliance evidence collection (SOC2/ISO).

Audience:
Platform engineers, infra SREs, security engineers, and solutions engineers who integrate Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments with customer networks.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to Redwood Private deployments (VPC-connected and air-gapped on-prem).
- Focused on network-level security plus transport auth (mTLS) for service-to-service comms.
- Not a full config reference; canonical configs live in infra-provisioning repo (linked above).

1) High-level VPC patterns (recommended)
Pattern A: Segmented VPC with proxy layer (recommended for most customers)
- Subnets:
  - mgmt-subnet (private, no internet egress) -> control plane components (operator, admin UIs)
  - ingress-subnet (public or NLB-facing private with NAT) -> boundary proxies / load balancers
  - compute-subnet(s) (private) -> inference nodes, model servers, KV caches
  - storage-subnet (private) -> block/object storage endpoints (S3 endpoint or on-prem storage network)
- Features:
  - Centralized NAT for egress (minimum necessary outbound destinations)
  - VPC Flow Logs enabled to collector (Kinesis/Logstash or direct to SIEM)
  - Private DNS zones for internal service discovery

Pattern B: Single-segment minimal VPC (for constrained networks)
- Single private subnet with strict SG rules; use host-based firewall and process-level mTLS to isolate services.
- Less ideal operationally; recommended only when customers require extremely small network footprint.

2) Ingress / egress controls (layered)
- Boundary (north-south) controls:
  - Use dedicated boundary proxies (Envoy/ALB/Nginx) that terminate TLS (or pass-through if customer requires mTLS to endpoint).
  - Minimize open public IPs; prefer private NLB + customer-managed ingress VPN or AWS PrivateLink.
- Egress controls:
  - Allowlist outbound destinations (container image registries, CRLs/OCSP endpoints, package mirrors, metrics/telemetry endpoints).
  - Use proxy for all egress traffic to enforce allowlist and TLS inspection where required.

3) Firewall / Security Group baseline (cloud-agnostic logical rules)
- Default-deny; only enable explicit allow rules.
- Management plane (ports allowed only from customer management CIDRs and Redwood support VPN):
  - 22 (SSH) - Disabled by default; enable via jumpbox and short-lived bastion with MFA only when absolutely necessary.
  - 3389 - Never open publicly.
  - 8443 / 443 - Control plane API - restrict to admin CIDRs and operator mTLS clients.
- Intra-VPC (service-to-service) rules:
  - Model serving nodes <-> KV cache: TCP 6379 (or configured port) - allow only from compute-subnet security group
  - Serving nodes <-> parameter server / weight store: allow specific ports (example 9200-9300) between groups, based on role.
  - Metrics/Tracing endpoints: ports restricted to telemetry collector group only.
- Example Security Group naming convention:
  - sg-controlplane-admin, sg-ingress-proxy, sg-compute-serving, sg-kv-cache, sg-telemetry-collector

4) mTLS design and operational guidance
Goals: mutual authentication between all internal services, encryption-in-transit, and automated rotation with minimal disruption.
- Certificate authority model:
  - Use an internal CA (HashiCorp Vault PKI or step-ca) per customer deployment. For air-gapped, run CA inside the customer VPC/cluster.
  - Root CA kept offline; intermediate CA issued for service certs and rotated regularly (90–180 day default).
- Certificate distribution:
  - Use a secrets injector (Vault Agent Injector / CSI driver) to mount short-lived certs into pods/hosts.
  - Avoid baking long-lived certs into images.
- Validation:
  - Enforce SAN-based validation; include service identity and deployment namespace in SANs.
  - Use SPIFFE IDs where possible (spiffe://redwood/customer/<deployment>/<service>).
- TLS profiles and cipher suites:
  - Enforce TLS1.2 minimum; prefer TLS1.3 for better performance and forward secrecy.
